algorithm.title: Calculating relative risk reduction (RRR) in clinical trials

nodes.text: Identify event rates: rate in control group (CER = 26%) and rate in intervention group (EER = 13%)
Calculate relative risk: RR = EER / CER = 13% / 26% = 0.50
Calculate relative risk reduction: RRR = (CER - EER) / CER = 50%
**Absolute risk reduction (ARR):** ARR = CER - EER = 26% - 13% = 13%
**Number needed to treat (NNT):** NNT = 1 / ARR = 1 / 0.13 = 7.7 patients

algorithm.title: Statistical power and type II error in small samples

nodes.text: Statistical power: probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when a true effect exists (Power = 1 - beta)
Type II error (beta): failing to detect a true difference when one actually exists (false-negative conclusion)

algorithm.title: Epidemiologic measures of association and excess risk

nodes.text: Cohort studies follow exposed and unexposed groups longitudinally to determine disease incidence
Incidence in exposed group: cases among exposed divided by total exposed individuals
Incidence in unexposed group: cases among unexposed divided by total unexposed individuals
Attributable risk (risk difference): excess risk in exposed calculated as exposed incidence minus unexposed incidence
**Relative risk (risk ratio):** ratio of incidence in exposed to unexposed
**Attributable risk percent (ARP):** proportion of disease in exposed attributable to exposure: (RR - 1) / RR
**Number needed to harm (NNH):** reciprocal of the attributable risk (1 / AR)

Calculate incidence in the unexposed group: cases in unexposed divided by total unexposed individuals
Relative risk (risk ratio) = incidence in exposed divided by incidence in unexposed
**Relative risk < 1.0:** exposure is associated with decreased risk of outcome (protective factor)
**Relative risk = 1.0:** null hypothesis accepted; no association between exposure and outcome
**Relative risk > 1.0:** exposure is associated with increased risk of outcome (harmful factor)

algorithm.title: Calculation of absolute risk reduction and number needed to treat

nodes.text: Control event rate: control events ÷ total control subjects
Treatment event rate: treatment events ÷ total treatment subjects
ARR = control rate − treatment rate = 0.333
NNT = 1 / ARR = 3
**NNT not a whole number:** round up to the next integer
**Treatment increases adverse effects:** NNH = 1 / absolute risk increase

n-10-q090.hinge: Length bias occurs when screening preferentially detects indolent, slow-growing tumors, artificially inflating survival.
n-10-q090.trap: Occupational cohort tempts healthy worker effect, but screening overestimation due to tumor biology is length bias.

nodes.text: Screening programs aim to detect asymptomatic disease early to reduce disease-specific mortality
Length-time bias: screening preferentially detects indolent, slowly progressive tumors with long preclinical phases
Result of length-time bias: overestimation of survival and screening benefit compared to aggressive interval cancers
**Lead-time bias:** early detection advances diagnosis date without prolonging actual survival
**Overdiagnosis bias:** detection of non-progressive lesions that would never have caused clinical disease
**Selection bias (healthy volunteer bias):** individuals adhering to screening have healthier baseline lifestyle habits
Randomized controlled trials with disease-specific mortality endpoints are required to prove screening benefit

abdominal-aortic-aneurysm.name: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
abdominal-aortic-aneurysm.scope: screening recommendations (men 65-75 who smoked), ultrasound imaging, surveillance intervals, elective repair thresholds, rupture
abdominal-aortic-aneurysm.core: Older adult with abdominal aortic dilation may remain asymptomatic until expansion or rupture; sudden abdominal/back pain and hypotension require immediate vascular rescue.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking strongest modifiable risk; older age, male sex, family history, hypertension, atherosclerosis
Women have higher rupture risk at smaller diameters; most aneurysms infrarenal
Existing AAA: **diameter and high BP** predict rupture; cholesterol, A1c do not

rows.label: Clues
items: Incidental pulsatile expansile abdominal mass; localized persistent pain suggests symptomatic aneurysm
Rupture triad incompletely present; transient stability may reflect contained retroperitoneal hemorrhage
Blue toe/distal ischemia may result from mural thrombus embolization
Acute back pain unchanged by movement = **referred pain**; prevertebral calcification on x-ray; not disc disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Medial elastin/collagen degradation → progressive enlargement; greater wall radius increases tension

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Abdominal ultrasound** diagnoses AAA, generally diameter ≥3 cm; no contrast required
★ Stable suspected rupture or preoperative planning → **CT angiography**
Unstable suspected rupture → bedside ultrasound if immediate; no CT transport delaying surgery
Ultrasound detects aneurysm but cannot reliably exclude rupture; follow symptoms/hemodynamics

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Rupture → **urgent vascular repair**, IV access, blood products; avoid delaying for complete workup
Permissive hypotension during transfer/resuscitation until hemorrhage control when clinically feasible
★ Elective repair: **≥5.5 cm men, ≥5.0 cm women**, symptoms; **not if short life expectancy** (metastatic cancer)
Rapid growth ≥0.5 cm/6 months → repair consideration; endovascular versus open based on anatomy/fitness
Smaller asymptomatic lesions → ultrasound surveillance below; refer vascular surgery, manage cardiovascular risks

rows.label: Complications
items: Rupture, thrombosis, distal embolization; repair → AKI, bowel ischemia, endoleak after EVAR
Aortoenteric fistula after prior graft: herald GI bleed → catastrophic hemorrhage; urgent evaluation

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ USPSTF: **one-time ultrasound men 65–75 who ever smoked**; selectively screen never-smoking men
Women never smoked/no family history → no screening; women smokers/family history → USPSTF evidence insufficient
Smoking cessation, BP control, statin for atherosclerotic disease; lifelong imaging follow-up after EVAR

rows.label: Mimics
items: Renal colic: flank-to-groin pain, hematuria; shock atypical
Aortic dissection: abrupt chest/back pain, possible pulse deficits or branch ischemia

abnormal-uterine-bleeding.name: Abnormal uterine bleeding
abnormal-uterine-bleeding.scope: Adenomyosis, leiomyomas, endometrial polyps, ovulatory dysfunction, PALM-COEIN classification, endometrial biopsy
abnormal-uterine-bleeding.core: Abnormal uterine bleeding requires pregnancy exclusion, hemodynamic assessment and evaluation for structural disease or unopposed endometrial estrogen.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Perimenopause, PCOS, obesity, anticoagulants; lifelong heavy bleeding suggests inherited coagulopathy
Adenomyosis often multiparous; fibroids common during reproductive years

rows.label: Clues
items: Bleeding affecting quality of life, prolonged/heavy menses, intermenstrual or irregular bleeding
Tachycardia, orthostasis or syncope → clinically important blood loss
Postmenopausal bleeding requires malignancy evaluation even with a single episode

rows.label: Pathophys
items: PALM: Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy/hyperplasia → structural causes
COEIN: Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not otherwise classified
Anovulation → absent cyclic progesterone, unopposed proliferation and unstable shedding
Combined OCPs → uniform estrogen/progestin exposure **synchronizes endometrium**, preventing irregular shedding

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pregnancy test and CBC** first; pelvic examination localizes uterine versus cervical/vaginal bleeding
**Transvaginal ultrasound** evaluates structural lesions; saline sonohysterography/hysteroscopy for intracavitary disease
★ **Endometrial biopsy ≥45 years**; younger with persistent bleeding, unopposed estrogen or failed treatment
Postmenopausal bleeding: endometrial thickness >4 mm → sampling; persistent bleeding → biopsy regardless of thickness
TSH for suspected endocrine disease; coagulation/vWF testing for suggestive bleeding history

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Unstable → IV access, blood resuscitation, urgent gynecology; tamponade or operative control if needed
Stable → high-dose combined OCP, progestin, tranexamic acid; no estrogen if prior VTE, hypertension, smoker >35
★ Long-term → **levonorgestrel IUD**, OCP/progestin; family complete, normal cavity → **ablation**; copper worsens
Fibroids: asymptomatic → **observation, any size**; symptomatic → myomectomy/embolization; hysterectomy if childbearing done
Polyp → hysteroscopic removal; adenomyosis refractory to hormones → hysterectomy

rows.label: Complications
items: Iron deficiency anemia; chronic anovulation → endometrial hyperplasia/cancer; structural lesions can impair fertility

rows.label: Prevention
items: Regular progestin exposure for chronic anovulation; replace iron and address metabolic drivers

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pregnancy complication: positive hCG; exclude ectopic pregnancy
Cervicitis: friable cervix and postcoital bleeding

table.title: Cause clues
rows: Firm irregular enlarged uterus; pressure symptoms
Labor-like pain, dilated os, beefy prolapsing tissue
Tender uterus; biopsy **plasma cells**, not neutrophils

acid-base-disorders.name: Acid-base disorders
acid-base-disorders.scope: Metabolic acidosis (anion gap, non-anion gap), metabolic alkalosis (saline-responsive vs saline-resistant), respiratory acidosis, respiratory alkalosis, Winter formula, mixed disorders
acid-base-disorders.core: Identify the primary pH disturbance, test expected compensation, then investigate the anion gap or urine chloride to locate the cause.

rows.label: Definition
items: Acidemia: pH <7.35; alkalemia: >7.45; normal pH can hide opposing primary disorders
Metabolic: primary HCO3 change; respiratory: primary PaCO2 change

rows.label: Formula
items: ★ **AG = Na − (Cl + HCO3)**; usual normal ≈8–12, laboratory dependent
Hypoalbuminemia correction: add 2.5 to AG per 1 g/dL albumin below 4
★ **Winter: expected PaCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3 + 8 ±2**

rows.label: Interpret
items: HCO3 12 → expected PaCO2 26 ±2; measured 40 → additional respiratory acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis: expected PaCO2 ≈40 + 0.7 × (HCO3 − 24), ±5
Respiratory HCO3 change per 10 PaCO2: acidosis +1 acute/+4 chronic; alkalosis −2 acute/−4 chronic

rows.label: Use when
items: ★ Alkalosis: **urine Cl <20 mmol/L** → saline-responsive; ≥20 → diuretics/mineralocorticoids
ΔAG exceeds HCO3 fall → additional alkalosis; smaller ΔAG → additional non-gap acidosis

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Compensation never overshoots; values outside expected range imply **mixed disorder**
Salicylates often cause respiratory alkalosis plus high-gap acidosis; near-normal pH is deceptive
Diarrhea/RTA: non-gap acidosis; distal RTA: urine pH >5.5, hypokalemia; renal failure: either gap pattern

acid-base-disorders.evidence: Established physiologic formulas; no guideline involved.

acute-coronary-syndromes.name: Acute coronary syndromes
acute-coronary-syndromes.scope: Unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI, cardiac biomarkers, risk stratification (HEART/TIMI), antiplatelet and anticoagulation, reperfusion
acute-coronary-syndromes.core: Acute myocardial ischemia from coronary plaque disruption: distinguish occlusive infarction needing immediate reperfusion from non-ST-elevation syndromes needing risk-guided invasive management.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, CKD, age, premature family CAD
Cocaine/stimulants, anemia, tachyarrhythmia may provoke ischemia; distinguish supply-demand injury from plaque rupture

rows.label: Clues
items: Pressure with arm/jaw radiation, diaphoresis, nausea; older adults/diabetes may have dyspnea or epigastric pain alone
Inferior MI with hypotension, clear lungs, raised JVP → suspect RV infarction
★ New murmur, pulmonary edema, shock after MI → **mechanical complication**, urgent echo
Unexplained crash/syncope + ischemic ECG → primary MI; troponin over trauma imaging

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Platelet activation and thrombin-mediated clot reduce coronary perfusion; necrosis releases troponin
Type 2 MI: oxygen mismatch without acute atherothrombosis; treat precipitating cause

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ECG within 10 minutes**, repeat if nondiagnostic; serial high-sensitivity troponin using validated pathway
Posterior suspicion → V7–V9; inferior MI → right-sided leads; new LBBB alone insufficient for STEMI
★ **Do not wait for troponin before STEMI reperfusion**; bedside echo if diagnosis/complications uncertain
HEART ≤3 + negative serial troponins → low risk; TIMI/GRACE stratifies NSTE-ACS
STE: **V1–V6 → LAD**; **II, III, aVF + bradycardia → RCA**; I, aVL → circumflex

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Chewed aspirin**, P2Y12 inhibitor, anticoagulant such as heparin, high-intensity atorvastatin; oxygen only if hypoxemic
Nitroglycerin (**venodilation** → ↓preload) for pain unless hypotension, RV infarction, recent PDE5 inhibitor; avoid NSAIDs
★ STEMI → **primary PCI** within 90 minutes at PCI center, ≤120 minutes including transfer
IF PCI delay >120 minutes, symptoms <12 hours, no contraindication → fibrinolysis promptly, then transfer

rows.label: Complications
items: VT/VF, AV block, HF, cardiogenic shock; free-wall rupture
Later aneurysm/thrombus, embolism, Dressler syndrome; antithrombotics → bleeding
Post-MI murmur: **papillary rupture** → apical, no O₂ step-up; **septal rupture** → left sternal, RA→RV step-up

rows.label: Prevention
items: DAPT usually 12 months after ACS unless bleeding risk changes plan; cardiac rehabilitation, smoking cessation
ACE inhibitor/ARB for LV dysfunction; beta-blocker when stable, avoid in shock or acute decompensation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Aortic dissection: abrupt tearing pain/pulse deficit; anticoagulation or lysis dangerous
Pericarditis: positional pleuritic pain, diffuse changes
PE: hypoxemia, thrombotic risk, RV strain

table.title: Syndrome branches
rows: Urgent catheterization if unstable; otherwise risk-guided angiography
Regional ST elevation or occlusion equivalent
Prior intracranial hemorrhage, active bleeding, suspected dissection
Stress or perfusion testing within 72 hours

acute-kidney-injury.name: Acute kidney injury
acute-kidney-injury.core: Abrupt loss of renal filtration: separate impaired perfusion, parenchymal injury, and urinary obstruction before treating the cause.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Volume depletion, sepsis, cirrhosis, low-output heart failure (prerenal despite overload); baseline CKD increases vulnerability
NSAIDs constrict afferent arterioles; ACE inhibitors/ARBs reduce efferent tone during hypoperfusion
Aminoglycosides, pigment (dipstick blood, few RBCs), prolonged ischemia → tubular damage; antibiotics/PPIs → tubulointerstitial inflammation

rows.label: Clues
items: Oliguria, edema, uremic nausea; urine output may remain normal
AIN: fever, rash, eosinophilia sometimes present; classic triad often absent
★ Pulmonary edema, severe hyperkalemia, encephalopathy, pericarditis → **urgent renal support**
Anuria despite patent catheter after pelvic surgery + hydronephrosis → ureteral injury/ligation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced glomerular pressure, tubular epithelial injury, or backpressure → declining GFR

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ AKI: creatinine ↑≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 h, ≥1.5-fold within 7 days, or oliguria
Oliguria criterion: urine <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥6 h; trend creatinine, electrolytes, fluid balance
★ **Urinalysis + microscopy**, medication review; bladder scan → renal ultrasound if obstruction possible
FeNa unreliable with diuretics, CKD, early obstruction; urine eosinophils neither sensitive nor specific
Unexplained persistent injury or suspected glomerulonephritis → nephrology, possible kidney biopsy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe hyperkalemia → **IV calcium**, insulin/dextrose; refractory electrolyte disturbance → dialysis
Hypovolemia (postoperative oliguria, high urine specific gravity) → saline bolus; congestion → loop diuretic; no reflex fluids in overload
Stop nephrotoxins, all NSAIDs including celecoxib (intra-articular steroid for joint pain); persistent AIN → glucocorticoids; renal-dose drugs
★ Obstruction → **catheter or ureteral decompression**; monitor postobstructive diuresis
Dialysis: refractory acidosis, hyperkalemia, intoxication, overload, symptomatic uremia; no isolated creatinine threshold

rows.label: Complications
items: Arrhythmias, acidosis, volume overload; subsequent CKD
Recovery diuresis → dehydration and electrolyte losses

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain perfusion during illness; review nephrotoxic combinations and monitor renal function
Contrast in high-risk CKD → **periprocedural IV isotonic saline**; diuretics, mannitol, metformin stop don't protect
ACR now limits contrast prophylaxis mainly to eGFR <30; older exam questions may expect wider hydration

rows.label: Mimics
items: CKD: longstanding abnormalities, small echogenic kidneys, chronic anemia
Trimethoprim effect: creatinine rise without true GFR decline

acute-kidney-injury.evidence: Not checked online; established KDIGO diagnostic criteria and renal teaching.

acute-rhinosinusitis.name: Acute rhinosinusitis
acute-rhinosinusitis.scope: Common cold, viral rhinosinusitis, acute bacterial rhinosinusitis criteria, symptomatic therapy, antibiotic stewardship
acute-rhinosinusitis.core: Acute nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, and facial pressure usually reflect a self-limited viral infection; duration and course identify likely bacterial disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Respiratory exposure, daycare contacts, impaired drainage from allergic inflammation
Immunocompromise, recent antibiotics, or hospitalization increases resistant-organism risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Cough, reduced smell, maxillary tenderness; colored mucus alone does not establish bacterial infection
★ Orbital swelling, painful eye movement, reduced vision, severe headache → **complicated infection**
Well febrile child, URI symptoms, clear lungs, good perfusion: soft flow murmur innocent, not VSD

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Viral mucosal edema blocks sinus drainage; secondary infection commonly pneumococcus, H influenzae, or Moraxella

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; uncomplicated illness needs neither sinus radiographs nor CT
Persistent, severe, or biphasic course identifies bacterial cases; fever alone is insufficient
Suspected orbital/intracranial extension → contrast CT; MRI for intracranial definition
Refractory or unusual infection → ENT evaluation; routine nasal swab cultures unhelpful

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Viral illness → **saline irrigation, acetaminophen/NSAID**, oral pseudoephedrine (not young children); no antibiotics
Intranasal fluticasone for associated allergic inflammation; topical oxymetazoline at most 3 days
★ Uncomplicated bacterial illness + reliable follow-up → **watchful waiting** or antibiotics
Antibiotic choice: amoxicillin-clavulanate, usually 5–7 days in adults; penicillin allergy → doxycycline
Complication → admission, IV ampicillin-sulbactam, urgent ENT/ophthalmology; avoid empiric azithromycin because resistance

rows.label: Complications
items: Orbital cellulitis or abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, intracranial abscess
Unnecessary antibiotics → diarrhea, C difficile, resistance

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hand hygiene, smoking avoidance, control allergic rhinitis
Sterile/distilled or previously boiled water for nasal irrigation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Allergic rhinitis: itching, sneezing, watery discharge without fever
Migraine: episodic disabling headache, photophobia, nausea
Dental infection: focal tooth pain, unilateral maxillary symptoms

table.title: Bacterial patterns
rows: Initial improvement → new fever or worsening symptoms

adrenal-insufficiency.name: Adrenal insufficiency
adrenal-insufficiency.scope: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), secondary adrenal insufficiency, cosyntropin stimulation test, morning serum cortisol, hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone replacement, adrenal crisis
adrenal-insufficiency.core: Weight loss, fatigue, orthostasis, and hyponatremia, or unexplained pressor-resistant shock after illness or interruption of glucocorticoids.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Primary: autoimmune destruction, TB, bilateral hemorrhage, metastases; associated autoimmune thyroid disease
★ Secondary: **prolonged glucocorticoids**, pituitary disease/surgery/apoplexy; abrupt withdrawal risks crisis
Crisis triggers: infection, trauma, surgery, missed replacement, vomiting

rows.label: Clues
items: Anorexia, abdominal pain, nausea, weakness; hypoglycemia, eosinophilia
Crisis: fever, confusion, severe volume depletion; symptoms may worsen rapidly during intercurrent illness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Cortisol deficiency reduces vascular catecholamine response and increases ADH
Primary gland failure removes mineralocorticoids; secondary disease retains renin–angiotensin-driven aldosterone

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **8 AM cortisol + ACTH**; very low cortisol supports, clearly high values argue against insufficiency
★ Equivocal basal cortisol → **cosyntropin (ACTH) stimulation**; inadequate assay-specific peak confirms impaired reserve
Traditional stimulated cutoff ≈18 µg/dL; newer assays may use ≈14–15; interpret laboratory standard
Primary → 21-hydroxylase antibodies, selected adrenal CT; secondary → pituitary evaluation/MRI
Recent pituitary injury may initially show normal cosyntropin response; clinical suspicion still matters

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Crisis → draw blood if feasible, **IV hydrocortisone + isotonic saline**, dextrose for hypoglycemia
Do not wait for confirmatory results; treat precipitant and correct electrolytes carefully
Coexisting hypothyroidism → glucocorticoid replacement before levothyroxine to avoid decompensation

rows.label: Complications
items: Untreated crisis → arrhythmia, circulatory collapse, death; chronic undertreatment → impaired function
Excess replacement → osteoporosis, diabetes, Cushingoid features

rows.label: Prevention
items: Stress-dose plan, emergency injectable hydrocortisone, medical alert ID; taper prolonged systemic steroids
Vomiting prevents absorption → parenteral replacement and urgent evaluation; teach sick-day plans to caregivers

rows.label: Mimics
items: SIADH: euvolemia, normal potassium and cortisol reserve
Sepsis: infection may coexist and trigger crisis
Hypothyroidism: bradycardia, cold intolerance, weight gain

table.title: Primary versus secondary
rows: Low/inappropriately normal ACTH; potassium usually normal

adrenal-insufficiency.evidence: Not checked online; established endocrine teaching; cortisol cutoffs are assay dependent.

adult-immunizations.name: Adult immunizations
adult-immunizations.scope: Routine adult vaccines, immunocompromised and HIV, pregnancy, live-vaccine contraindications, chronic medical conditions (COPD, diabetes, liver disease), vaccine counseling and addressing hesitancy
adult-immunizations.core: Match vaccination to age, prior doses, pregnancy, immune status, and exposure risk; missed series resume without restarting.

rows.label: Who
items: ★ **HepB**: all 19–59; ≥60 with risk/request; health worker anti-HBs negative post-series → revaccinate
**HIV any CD4**, liver disease/alcohol, COPD, diabetes, smoking → pneumococcal <50; liver → HepA/HepB
Asplenia → pneumococcal, MenACWY, MenB, Hib; HIV → MenACWY

rows.label: Start/stop
items: ★ Pregnancy: **Tdap each pregnancy at 27–36 wk**; inactivated influenza any trimester
Maternal RSV: Abrysvo at 32–36 wk, September–January; previous pregnancy dose → infant antibody instead
RSV once: all ≥75; ages 50–74 with increased severe-disease risk

rows.label: Test
items: Anti-HBs/anti-HAV/VZV IgG positive → immune, skip; otherwise **do not delay vaccination** for serology
★ Immunocompromised ≥19 → recombinant zoster; HIV CD4 ≥200 permits MMR/varicella if nonimmune
HPV started <15 → two doses; ≥15 or immunocompromised → three

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **No live MMR, varicella, intranasal influenza**: severe immunosuppression, pregnancy (nonimmune → postpartum)
PCV15 → PPSV23: ≥8 weeks immunocompromised; older exams: PPSV23 alone; mild illness/antibiotics: no deferral
Hesitancy → elicit concern; inactivated influenza cannot cause flu, coincidental virus; refusal → document, revisit

table.title: Routine adult schedule
rows: Annual influenza; updated COVID-19 for all adults
Tdap once, then either every 10 years
PCV20/21 alone; PCV15 → PPSV23 after 1 year

alcohol-withdrawal.name: Alcohol withdrawal
alcohol-withdrawal.core: Autonomic and neuropsychiatric excitation after reducing prolonged heavy alcohol intake; progression from mild symptoms to life-threatening delirium.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior withdrawal seizures/delirium, repeated detoxifications, heavy sustained use, older age
Acute illness, electrolyte depletion, concurrent sedative dependence; poor support increases outpatient failure

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, insomnia, nausea; symptoms possible with **positive blood alcohol**
Hospital day 2–5 or postoperative: new agitation, hallucinations, autonomic signs → suspect **unreported alcohol use**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Chronic ethanol → downregulated GABA inhibition/upregulated NMDA excitation; cessation unmasks neuronal hyperactivity
Repeated episodes → kindling, progressively lower seizure threshold

rows.label: Dx
items: **Clinical diagnosis** + time since reduction; bedside glucose, CBC, electrolytes, Mg, phosphate, liver tests
★ **CIWA-Ar** if communicative; ≥19 severe; delirium/intubation → **RASS/MINDS**
First/focal seizure, head injury, focal deficit, atypical timing → head CT; do not assume withdrawal

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Diazepam/chlordiazepoxide** symptom-triggered; liver dysfunction/older frail adults → **lorazepam/oxazepam**
★ Seizures/delirium → monitored inpatient **IV benzodiazepines**; refractory → ICU phenobarbital with respiratory monitoring
★ **Parenteral thiamine**; hypoglycemia → immediate dextrose, never wait; correct electrolyte deficits
Phenytoin ineffective; dexmedetomidine adjunct; **chlorpromazine**/antipsychotics lower seizure threshold, prolong QT

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration, dysrhythmias, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis; excessive sedation → respiratory depression
Malnutrition → Wernicke encephalopathy: confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia; suspected → high-dose IV thiamine
Pregnancy: seizures, adrenergic surge → fetal hypoxia; **maternal withdrawal** is greatest immediate fetal risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: High-risk inpatients → preventive benzodiazepines; outpatient withdrawal only if mild, reliable supervision
Recovery: **naltrexone** unless opioids/acute hepatitis; **acamprosate** unless severe CKD; addiction follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hepatic encephalopathy: asterixis, decompensated cirrhosis, less autonomic excitation
Sepsis: infectious source, hypotension, persistent inflammatory findings
Sedative withdrawal: benzodiazepine/barbiturate reduction; similar syndrome, different exposure
Anticholinergic delirium: dry skin, urinary retention; diaphoresis favors withdrawal

table.title: Approximate onset after reduction; overlap common
rows: Visual/auditory/tactile hallucinations; clear sensorium; vitals near normal
Disorientation, hallucinations, fever, tremor, marked autonomic instability

anaphylaxis.name: Anaphylaxis
anaphylaxis.scope: Anaphylaxis, angioedema, biphasic reactions, epinephrine autoinjector, emergency airway management
anaphylaxis.core: Rapid multisystem reaction after exposure—or isolated hypotension or airway compromise after a known allergen—requires epinephrine immediately.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Foods, insect venom, antibiotics, latex; exercise can amplify food-triggered reactions
Asthma, prior severe reaction, mast-cell disorders; beta-blockers can complicate treatment

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Urticaria/angioedema + wheeze, stridor, hypotension, or severe GI symptoms**
Skin findings may be absent; hoarseness and tongue swelling predict airway danger
Biphasic recurrence after apparent resolution, especially after severe or undertreated episodes

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mast-cell/basophil mediators → vasodilation, capillary leak, bronchoconstriction; often IgE-mediated
Epinephrine: α1 reverses vasodilation/edema, β2 reverses bronchoconstriction; albuterol alone misses edema and shock

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; never wait for tryptase or laboratory confirmation
Acute and baseline serum tryptase can support uncertain cases; normal results do not exclude anaphylaxis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **IM epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg**, adult 0.3–0.5 mg, lateral thigh; repeat every 5–15 minutes
Supine with legs elevated unless respiratory distress; oxygen, early intubation for progressive obstruction
Profound shock or refractory hypotension → titrated IV epinephrine plus **isotonic boluses**; beta-blocker use → glucagon
Albuterol for residual bronchospasm; antihistamines relieve itching only; steroids do not reliably prevent biphasic reactions
★ Monitor until resolved; **longer observation/admission** after hypotension, repeated epinephrine, or severe asthma

rows.label: Complications
items: Asphyxia, distributive shock, arrhythmia, hypoxic brain injury
Undiluted IV epinephrine bolus errors → ischemia and dangerous dysrhythmia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Prescribe **epinephrine autoinjector**, demonstrate technique, provide written action plan and allergy referral
Extra device for repeat-dose risk; avoidance, medical alert ID; venom immunotherapy after qualifying sting allergy

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vasovagal episode: bradycardia, pallor, rapid improvement supine
Bradykinin angioedema: no itching/hives; ACE inhibitor or hereditary disease → airway, icatibant/C1 inhibitor

antepartum-bleeding.name: Antepartum bleeding
antepartum-bleeding.scope: Placenta previa, placental abruption, vasa previa, uterine rupture, transabdominal ultrasound before digital exam, Kleihauer-Betke test, emergent cesarean delivery
antepartum-bleeding.core: Bleeding in later pregnancy requires immediate maternal stabilization and fetal assessment, followed by placental localization before any digital cervical examination.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Previa: prior cesarean, multiparity; abruption: hypertension, cocaine, trauma, prior abruption
Vasa previa: velamentous cord, accessory placental lobe, IVF; rupture: uterine scar, obstructed labor

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Shock may exceed visible blood loss** with concealed abruption or internal hemorrhage
Assess uterine tone, pain, contractions, fetal tracing, membrane status; bleeding volume alone is unreliable

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Maternal placental bleeding versus fetal vessel hemorrhage; vasa previa can rapidly exsanguinate fetus
Placental separation or uterine disruption compromises oxygen delivery independent of maternal external blood loss

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ CBC, type/crossmatch, coagulation studies including fibrinogen; continuous fetal monitoring if viable
★ **Ultrasound before digital examination**; transabdominal first; transvaginal safely clarifies placenta–cervix relationship
Normal ultrasound does not exclude abruption; suspected rupture is a clinical emergency
Rh-negative bleeding/trauma → Kleihauer–Betke or flow cytometry quantifies fetomaternal hemorrhage for anti-D dosing

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ ABCs, two large IVs, blood products when needed; **do not delay delivery for imaging if unstable**
Hemorrhage/fetal compromise → emergency cesarean; rupture → laparotomy, uterine repair or hysterectomy
Stable preterm previa → observation, pelvic rest, corticosteroids when eligible; planned cesarean before labor
Abruption: deliver if significant or compromised; vaginal birth possible when stable and imminent or fetal demise
Unsensitized Rh-negative patient → anti-D immunoglobulin; correct abruption-associated coagulopathy

rows.label: Complications
items: Hemorrhagic shock, DIC, AKI, hysterectomy; fetal hypoxia, death, prematurity
Previa plus cesarean scar increases placenta accreta spectrum risk and operative hemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: Control BP, avoid cocaine/tobacco; prenatal placental/cord localization and planned high-risk delivery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Bloody show: small mucus-streaked bleeding with cervical change
Cervical lesion: contact bleeding, visible source on speculum examination

table.title: Critical distinctions
rows: Bleeding after rupture; sudden fetal bradycardia
Scarred uterus; sudden pain, lost station, fetal bradycardia

antepartum-bleeding.evidence: Not checked online; established obstetric hemorrhage teaching.

antepartum-fetal-surveillance.name: Antepartum fetal surveillance
antepartum-fetal-surveillance.scope: Nonstress test (reactive vs nonreactive), biophysical profile (BPP components and scoring), modified BPP, contraction stress test, umbilical artery Doppler, indications (FGR, diabetes, post-term, decreased movement)
antepartum-fetal-surveillance.core: Assess fetal well-being when stillbirth risk is elevated; abnormal screening generally needs confirmation or delivery according to gestation and severity.

rows.label: Who
items: ★ FGR, high-risk diabetes, hypertension, post-term pregnancy, decreased fetal movement

rows.label: Start/stop
items: Often around 32 weeks; earlier if severe risk and delivery would be considered
Decreased movement → prompt NST/fluid assessment; ongoing frequency based on underlying disorder

rows.label: Test
items: ★ Reactive NST ≥32 weeks: **two 15-beat accelerations lasting 15 seconds**, within 20 minutes
Before 32 weeks use 10 × 10; extend observation to 40 minutes for sleep
★ **BPP**: NST plus four ultrasound components; each 0 or 2, maximum 10

rows.label: IF positive
items: Nonreactive NST → stimulation/extended tracing, then BPP or selected contraction stress test
★ BPP ≤4 generally → delivery; 6 → repeat within 24 hours or term delivery
Low fluid requires evaluation despite score; umbilical Doppler guides FGR decisions

rows.label: Traps
items: BPP 8–10 reassuring only with normal fluid; modified BPP = NST + fluid assessment
CST: late decelerations with ≥50% contractions positive; avoid when labor contraindicated
False positives common; reassuring test does not predict acute abruption or cord accident

table.title: Ultrasound BPP: normal criteria during 30-minute observation

antepartum-fetal-surveillance.evidence: Indications checked 2026-10-30: [ACOG surveillance guidance](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2021/06/indications-for-outpatient-antenatal-fetal-surveillance); interpretation established obstetric teaching.

anticholinergic-toxicity.name: Anticholinergic toxicity
anticholinergic-toxicity.scope: Antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants, atropine, anticholinergic toxidrome, physostigmine
anticholinergic-toxicity.core: Delirium with mydriasis, dry flushed skin, hyperthermia, urinary retention, and reduced bowel sounds after muscarinic blockade.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Diphenhydramine, first-generation antihistamines in OTC cold/sleep products, atropine, scopolamine, tricyclic antidepressants, toxic plants
Benztropine, trihexyphenidyl for parkinsonism/EPS; chlorpromazine and other low-potency antipsychotics
Older age, polypharmacy, accidental pediatric ingestion, intentional overdose; mixed toxidromes are common

rows.label: Clues
items: Agitation, hallucinations, picking at unseen objects, blurred vision, tachycardia
★ **Hot and dry**, rather than sweaty; severe poisoning causes seizures, coma, dysrhythmias
Palpable bladder, ileus; TCA exposure may add hypotension and conduction abnormalities

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Central/peripheral muscarinic antagonism; some causative drugs also block sodium channels
Absent sweating impairs heat dissipation; agitation further increases temperature
Muscarinic blockade → ↓**detrusor tone** → urinary retention; ↓gut motility → constipation/ileus

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical toxidrome + ECG**; check QRS/QTc before considering reversal
Glucose, electrolytes, creatinine, CK; acetaminophen level for uncertain intentional ingestion
TCA markers: QRS >100 ms or terminal R in aVR signals sodium-channel toxicity
Drug screens do not establish severity; ECG and physiology drive treatment

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Airway support, IV fluids, external cooling; **benzodiazepines** for agitation/seizures
**Stop offending drug** first; bladder catheter for retention; charcoal early only with protected airway
★ Pure severe antimuscarinic delirium → selected **physostigmine**, slow IV with continuous monitoring and expert supervision
Avoid physostigmine with suspected TCA/mixed cardiotoxic ingestion, QRS widening, significant conduction disease, or seizures
Sodium-channel blockade → **IV sodium bicarbonate**; avoid QT-prolonging antipsychotics in high-risk poisoning

rows.label: Complications
items: Rhabdomyolysis, AKI, aspiration, heat injury, ventricular arrhythmia, death
Physostigmine → bradycardia, seizures, asystole in unsuitable patients

rows.label: Prevention
items: Reduce anticholinergic burden, safe storage, avoid duplicate OTC sleep/cold products; assess intent after stabilization

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sympathomimetic toxicity: diaphoresis and active bowel sounds
Serotonin syndrome: clonus, hyperreflexia, diarrhea
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: lead-pipe rigidity, dopamine-blocker exposure

anticholinergic-toxicity.evidence: Not checked online; established emergency toxicology teaching.

antidepressants.name: Antidepressants
antidepressants.scope: SSRIs, SNRIs, bupropion, mirtazapine, tricyclic antidepressants (anticholinergic toxicity, urinary retention, arrhythmia), MAO inhibitors, adverse effects (serotonin syndrome)
antidepressants.core: SSRIs usually start depression treatment; choose alternatives by accompanying symptoms, adverse effects, and overdose risk.

rows.label: Use
items: SSRIs/SNRIs: depression, anxiety; duloxetine also neuropathic pain
Bupropion: smoking cessation; mirtazapine: poor appetite with insomnia
TCAs/MAOIs: resistant depression; TCAs also neuropathic pain

rows.label: Mechanism
items: SSRIs: serotonin reuptake blockade; SNRIs/TCAs: serotonin + norepinephrine reuptake blockade
Bupropion: norepinephrine/dopamine reuptake blockade; mirtazapine: α2 antagonism
MAOIs: reduced monoamine degradation

rows.label: Adverse
items: SSRIs: GI upset, SIADH, bleeding; SNRIs: ↑BP; mirtazapine: sedation/weight gain; bupropion: activating
★ SSRI **sexual dysfunction** → **lower dose** first; other SSRIs rarely help; bupropion minimal
TCAs: constipation, urinary retention, conduction toxicity; MAOIs: orthostatic hypotension

rows.label: Avoid
items: ★ Bupropion lowers seizure threshold: **seizure or eating disorders**; CYP inhibitors raise levels
TCAs: urinary retention, glaucoma, conduction disease; anticholinergic delirium in older adults
TCA therapy with QTc/QRS prolongation → **stop TCA**, no waiting for levels

rows.label: Interactions
items: MAOI + tyramine/sympathomimetics → hypertensive crisis → **phentolamine** (α-blocker)
MAOI + SSRI/tramadol → serotonin syndrome; washout generally 14 days, after fluoxetine 5 weeks
Fluoxetine/paroxetine inhibit CYP2D6 → ↑TCA levels, toxicity

rows.label: Monitor
items: Mood, suicidality early in young adults; monitor adherence and functioning
Abrupt stop → **discontinuation**: flu-like aches, headache, dizziness, electric paresthesias, nausea, tremor
Response over 4–6 weeks; taper to stop, especially paroxetine and venlafaxine

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Serotonin syndrome**: clonus, fever/agitation → stop drugs, benzodiazepines; cyproheptadine
★ TCA overdose: Na⁺-channel blockade → **wide QRS**, arrhythmia, seizures → IV sodium bicarbonate
Bipolar depression: antidepressant monotherapy may provoke mania

antidepressants.evidence: Not checked online; established pharmacology and prescribing safety.

asplenia.name: Asplenia
asplenia.scope: Anatomic asplenia (splenectomy), functional asplenia (sickle cell), Howell-Jolly bodies, reactive thrombocytosis, encapsulated organism sepsis (Streptococcus pneumoniae), vaccination timing, antibiotic prophylaxis
asplenia.core: Absent or poorly functioning spleen impairs clearance of encapsulated organisms; fever can progress rapidly to fatal sepsis despite prior vaccination.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Splenectomy for trauma/hematologic disease; functional loss with sickle cell disease; congenital absence
Sepsis risk greatest early after surgery and in children, but remains lifelong

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Fever, rigors, malaise, vomiting, or rapid deterioration → **overwhelming postsplenectomy infection**
Pneumococcus especially important; also meningococcus, Hib; dog bites risk Capnocytophaga
Travel-associated malaria and Babesia can become unusually severe

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Loss of splenic macrophage filtration and IgM memory B-cell function impairs opsonized-organism clearance
Reduced removal of erythrocyte inclusions and platelets explains characteristic blood findings

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Smear: **Howell–Jolly bodies**; reactive thrombocytosis after splenectomy; correlate with history/imaging
Febrile illness → cultures, CBC, lactate, source evaluation; do not delay antibiotics for results
Unexplained anemia/fever after tick exposure or travel → smear/PCR for intraerythrocytic parasites

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected sepsis → **immediate ceftriaxone**, add vancomycin for severe/resistant pneumococcal concern
Resuscitate and admit if ill; even initially mild fever requires urgent clinical evaluation
Standby oral antibiotic if immediate care inaccessible, followed by emergency evaluation; not a substitute for assessment
Daily penicillin/amoxicillin in young children, particularly sickle cell disease through at least age 5

rows.label: Complications
items: Fulminant bacteremia, meningitis, purpura fulminans, DIC, death
Postoperative thrombosis risk; isolated reactive platelet elevation does not automatically require antiplatelet treatment

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Vaccinate **≥14 days before elective splenectomy**; after emergency surgery vaccinate once stable
Adult antibiotic prophylaxis individualized by postoperative period, immune status, and prior invasive infection
Medical alert ID, fever plan, influenza vaccination; bite counseling, travel precautions and malaria prevention

rows.label: Mimics
items: Iron deficiency: reactive thrombocytosis without splenic dysfunction
Hyposplenism: spleen present but impaired; similar infection precautions

table.title: Vaccine priorities: unvaccinated adults
rows: One dose if not previously vaccinated

asthma.name: Asthma
asthma.scope: Diagnosis, stepwise therapy, acute exacerbation, exercise-induced bronchoconstriction
asthma.core: Variable episodes of wheeze, cough, dyspnea, and chest tightness from reversible expiratory airflow limitation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: **Family history of asthma/atopy**: strongest childhood risk; allergens, viral infections, smoke, occupational sensitizers
Exercise/cold air, aspirin-sensitive disease, nonselective beta-blockers; assess workplace symptom pattern

rows.label: Clues
items: Nocturnal/early-morning symptoms; normal examination between attacks
★ **Silent chest, exhaustion, altered mentation, rising PaCO2** → impending respiratory failure
Acute attack: low peak flow, accessory-muscle use, difficulty speaking
Cough-variant: isolated chronic cough, worse with cold/exercise; normal examination and radiograph

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Allergen cross-links IgE on **mast cells** → histamine, leukotrienes → bronchoconstriction
Airway inflammation, smooth-muscle constriction, mucus → variable obstruction and hyperresponsiveness
Persistent uncontrolled inflammation → remodeling with incompletely reversible airflow limitation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Spirometry**: obstruction with bronchodilator FEV1 increase >12% and >200 mL in adults
Normal spirometry with suspicion → repeat during symptoms or methacholine challenge
Exercise challenge: postexercise FEV1 fall >10%; assess baseline control before isolated exercise diagnosis
PFT pattern: ↓FEV1, normal/↓FVC, normal/↑TLC from air trapping

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Exacerbation → **repeated inhaled albuterol + ipratropium**, oxygen, early systemic glucocorticoids
Severe poor response → IV magnesium; deterioration → intubation; avoid sedatives and routine antibiotics
Exercise symptoms → preexercise albuterol or prescribed ICS-formoterol; persistent symptoms → improve controller
Check technique/adherence before stepping up; uncontrolled despite high-dose ICS-LABA → phenotype-directed biologic referral
Discharge: **PEF ≥70–80% predicted** (less wheeze is unreliable) + 5–7 day **oral prednisone** prevents relapse

rows.label: Complications
items: Status asthmaticus, pneumothorax, respiratory arrest
ICS → thrush/dysphonia; systemic steroids → osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, adrenal suppression

rows.label: Prevention
items: Written action plan, trigger reduction, smoking cessation, spacer; rinse mouth after ICS
★ GINA: **no SABA-only treatment**, no LABA monotherapy; ICS with every reliever use
Older exam questions (NAEPP) may expect: symptoms ≤2 days/week, awakenings ≤2/month → **SABA alone**; more → daily ICS

rows.label: Mimics
items: Inducible laryngeal obstruction: inspiratory stridor, inspiratory flow-loop flattening
COPD: persistent obstruction, smoking history
HF: edema, elevated JVP, cardiac findings
Deconditioning: obese/sedentary, exertional dyspnea; normal PFTs, no bronchodilator response

atheroembolic-disease.name: Atheroembolic disease
atheroembolic-disease.scope: Cholesterol crystal embolization, vascular procedures, livedo reticularis, blue toe syndrome, acute kidney injury, eosinophilia and hypocomplementemia, supportive management
atheroembolic-disease.core: Delayed kidney injury plus livedo reticularis or painful blue toes after arterial instrumentation suggests cholesterol crystal embolization.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Extensive aortic atherosclerosis, older age, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, peripheral arterial disease
★ Recent **angiography, vascular surgery**, or aortic manipulation; occasionally spontaneous plaque disruption
Anticoagulation/thrombolysis may precipitate embolization but do not establish the diagnosis alone

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Intact distal pulses** despite digital ischemia; multifocal skin findings
Creatinine rises days to weeks after exposure rather than immediately
Eosinophilia, hypocomplementemia, elevated ESR; urinalysis often bland or mildly proteinuric/hematuric
Retinal cholesterol plaques, abdominal pain, GI bleeding, or neurologic deficits indicate additional organs involved

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Plaque rupture releases cholesterol crystals into small arteries and arterioles
Mechanical occlusion plus foreign-body inflammation → progressive downstream tissue injury

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Characteristic clinical pattern often sufficient; review procedure timing and multisystem signs
Uncertain diagnosis → **skin biopsy** of accessible affected tissue; renal biopsy if needed
Histology: empty needle-shaped cholesterol clefts within occluded vessels; crystals dissolve during processing
Assess renal function, electrolytes, urinalysis; ultrasound excludes coincident obstructive renal injury

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Supportive care**: manage BP, volume, electrolytes; dialysis for conventional urgent indications
High-intensity statin and vascular risk reduction; antiplatelet treatment for underlying atherosclerotic indications
Avoid further aortic instrumentation when possible; no routine thrombolysis or anticoagulation for crystal emboli
Continue anticoagulation only for compelling separate indications; routine corticosteroids lack established benefit

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent kidney dysfunction, dialysis dependence, digital necrosis, bowel ischemia
Extensive systemic embolization → multiorgan failure and death

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, lipid/BP/diabetes control; minimize unnecessary arterial procedures in severe aortic disease
Use less invasive vascular evaluation when sufficient; monitor renal function after high-risk interventions

rows.label: Mimics
items: Contrast-associated AKI: onset within 24–72 hours, usually improves; no systemic embolic skin signs
Acute arterial thromboembolism: abrupt limb ischemia with diminished pulses
Vasculitis: inflammatory vessel injury, often active urine sediment; biopsy lacks cholesterol clefts

atheroembolic-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established cholesterol-embolization teaching.

atrial-fibrillation.name: Atrial fibrillation
atrial-fibrillation.scope: Rate and rhythm control, stroke prevention (CHA2DS2-VASc), unstable AF, embolic complications
atrial-fibrillation.core: Disorganized atrial activation produces an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm and left atrial appendage thromboembolism risk.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, hypertension, heart failure, coronary disease, obesity, sleep apnea
Hyperthyroidism, alcohol binges, infection, postoperative stress, mitral valve disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Palpitations, exercise intolerance, dyspnea; sometimes incidental or first detected after stroke
★ **Hypotension, ischemic chest pain, pulmonary edema, altered mentation** → unstable AF
Very rapid irregular wide-complex rhythm suggests preexcitation; ordinary AV nodal blockers can be dangerous

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Pulmonary-vein ectopic triggers plus atrial remodeling sustain reentry
Loss of atrial contraction reduces filling; persistent tachycardia can impair LV function

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ECG: absent discrete P waves**, variable RR intervals; document rhythm rather than pulse alone
TSH, electrolytes, renal function; transthoracic echocardiogram for ventricular function and structural disease
Intermittent symptoms → ambulatory rhythm monitoring; assess reversible triggers

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Unstable → **synchronized cardioversion**; do not delay for anticoagulation or TEE
Stable rate control: metoprolol or diltiazem; avoid diltiazem/verapamil with reduced EF
Decompensated HF: digoxin or amiodarone; preexcited AF: procainamide or cardioversion, no AV nodal blockers
Rhythm control for symptoms, early disease, or HF: cardioversion, selected antiarrhythmics, catheter ablation
★ Duration ≥48 hours/unknown: **3 weeks anticoagulation or TEE** before elective cardioversion; ≥4 weeks afterward

rows.label: Complications
items: **Top risk factor for cardioembolic stroke**, above age/hypertension; limb/gut emboli; tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy
Anticoagulant bleeding; rhythm drugs may cause proarrhythmia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Long-term anticoagulation: **CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 men/≥3 women**; consider one point lower
Apixaban/other DOAC preferred; mechanical valve or moderate/severe rheumatic mitral stenosis → warfarin
Weight reduction, BP/OSA treatment, limit alcohol
Aspirin no substitute for anticoagulation; adding aspirin to warfarin/DOAC → **more bleeding**, no added stroke protection

rows.label: Mimics
items: Atrial flutter: sawtooth atrial activity, often regular 2:1 conduction
Multifocal atrial tachycardia: ≥3 P-wave morphologies, isoelectric intervals

autoimmune-biliary-diseases.name: Autoimmune biliary diseases
autoimmune-biliary-diseases.scope: Primary sclerosing cholangitis, primary biliary cholangitis, bead-like strictures on MRCP, AMA, ursodeoxycholic acid
autoimmune-biliary-diseases.core: Chronic cholestasis with pruritus and fatigue suggests immune-mediated bile-duct disease; anatomy and serology distinguish the major types.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Coexisting autoimmune disease; family susceptibility
PSC strongly associated with ulcerative colitis, progresses despite colectomy; PBC usually middle-aged women

rows.label: Clues
items: Disproportionate ALP/GGT elevation; bilirubin may remain normal early
Excoriations, jaundice, hepatomegaly; xanthelasma and fat malabsorption with prolonged cholestasis
★ Fever, RUQ pain, new jaundice → **acute bacterial cholangitis**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Chronic duct injury → impaired bile flow, progressive fibrosis and biliary cirrhosis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Cholestatic labs → **RUQ ultrasound** first to exclude mechanical obstruction
PBC usually diagnosed with cholestasis plus disease-specific antibodies; biopsy if atypical/seronegative
PSC with normal cholangiogram and persistent suspicion → biopsy for small-duct disease
New dominant/relevant stricture → ERCP with sampling for cholangiocarcinoma; not routine diagnostic ERCP

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Ursodeoxycholic acid** first-line PBC; inadequate response/intolerance → seladelpar or elafibranor
PSC: no established disease-modifying drug; avoid high-dose ursodeoxycholic acid
Bacterial cholangitis → antibiotics and biliary drainage; obstructive stricture → endoscopic intervention
Cholestyramine for itch; advanced decompensation or refractory symptoms → liver transplant
Obeticholic acid withdrawn in US 2025 → not a current second-line choice

rows.label: Complications
items: Portal hypertension, hepatic failure, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, osteoporosis
PSC → cholangiocarcinoma, gallbladder cancer, colorectal cancer with IBD

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Bone-density assessment, vitamin replacement when deficient; hepatitis A/B vaccination
PSC → colonoscopy for occult IBD and ongoing cancer surveillance; cirrhosis → HCC surveillance

rows.label: Mimics
items: Choledocholithiasis: discrete obstructing stone; IgG4 cholangitis: pancreatic disease, steroid responsiveness
Drug cholestasis: temporal drug exposure without characteristic chronic duct findings

bell-palsy.name: Bell palsy
bell-palsy.scope: Idiopathic facial nerve (CN VII) palsy, forehead involvement vs central sparing, eye care, oral glucocorticoids, Lyme disease facial palsy
bell-palsy.core: Acute unilateral peripheral facial weakness includes the forehead; protect the cornea and treat early after excluding secondary causes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pregnancy/postpartum period, diabetes; often follows viral illness
Tick exposure/endemic region suggests Lyme; otalgia with vesicles suggests varicella-zoster

rows.label: Clues
items: Rapid onset over hours, maximal within 72 hours; drooping mouth and incomplete eyelid closure
Flattened nasolabial fold, impaired taste anterior tongue, hyperacusis; otherwise normal neurologic examination
★ Limb weakness, aphasia, diplopia or ataxia → **stroke/brainstem lesion evaluation**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inflammation and edema of CN VII within facial canal impair ipsilateral facial muscles
Supranuclear lesions usually spare upper facial movement because of bilateral cortical innervation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; document forehead movement, eye closure, ear findings and other cranial nerves
Lyme serology for compatible exposure, bilateral palsy, meningitic symptoms or systemic features
MRI for progressive, recurrent same-side, atypical or persistent palsy; no routine imaging for typical presentation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Oral prednisone within 72 hours**; consider added valacyclovir for severe/complete paralysis
★ **Artificial tears**, nighttime eye ointment and taping; urgent ophthalmology for corneal injury
Lyme-associated palsy → doxycycline or ceftriaxone according to neurologic involvement; steroid benefit uncertain
Ramsay Hunt syndrome → valacyclovir plus glucocorticoid; antivirals alone insufficient for idiopathic palsy

rows.label: Complications
items: Exposure keratitis/ulceration, synkinesis, facial contracture, incomplete recovery
Aberrant reinnervation → crocodile tears during eating

rows.label: Prevention
items: Tick avoidance reduces Lyme-associated disease; no proven primary prevention for idiopathic episodes

rows.label: Mimics
items: Central hemispheric stroke: contralateral lower-face weakness, forehead usually spared
Parotid tumor: gradual progression or palpable mass; otitis: infectious ear findings

bell-palsy.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

bladder-cancer.name: Bladder cancer
bladder-cancer.scope: Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, painless gross hematuria, smoking and occupational exposures, cystoscopy, transurethral resection
bladder-cancer.core: Painless gross hematuria in an older adult requires evaluation for urinary tract malignancy, even during anticoagulation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Smoking**, aromatic amines in dye/rubber industries; older age and male sex
Cyclophosphamide, pelvic radiation; chronic catheter irritation and Schistosoma haematobium predispose to squamous carcinoma

rows.label: Clues
items: Intermittent bleeding, clots; carcinoma in situ may produce irritative voiding symptoms without a visible mass
Advanced disease: pelvic pain, hydronephrosis, weight loss, or bone pain

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Urothelial field injury → multifocal tumors and recurrence throughout the collecting system
Squamous metaplasia from chronic inflammation → keratinizing malignancy

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Cystoscopy + CT urography** evaluate bladder and upper tracts; urinalysis/culture assess alternatives
Urine cytology helps detect high-grade disease/CIS; negative cytology does not exclude cancer
★ **TURBT including muscularis propria** establishes histology, grade, and depth
T1 disease → repeat resection within 6 weeks; invasive disease → chest/abdomen/pelvis staging

rows.label: Tx
items: Clot retention → large-bore catheter, irrigation; persistent obstruction or bleeding → urgent urology
Selected fit patients seeking bladder preservation → maximal resection plus concurrent chemoradiation
Avoid intravesical chemotherapy with suspected bladder perforation; BCG contraindicated during active symptomatic UTI

rows.label: Complications
items: Obstructive renal failure, recurrent hemorrhage, nodal or distant metastases
Intravesical BCG → cystitis; rarely disseminated infection; cystectomy → diversion-related metabolic complications

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation and occupational protection; no routine population screening
★ **Surveillance cystoscopy** after treatment because recurrence is common; interval based on risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nephrolithiasis: colicky flank pain, stone on noncontrast CT
Glomerulonephritis: dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, proteinuria
Cystitis: dysuria and positive culture; persistent hematuria after treatment still needs evaluation
Urethral carcinoma: older woman, blood spotting, friable urethral meatal mass, irritative/obstructive voiding

table.title: Depth determines definitive treatment
rows: TURBT + intravesical BCG; selected early cystectomy

bone-tumors.name: Bone tumors
bone-tumors.scope: Osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, chondrosarcoma, giant cell tumor of bone, osteochondroma, osteoid osteoma, bone metastases, biopsy
bone-tumors.core: Persistent focal bone pain, a growing mass, or a destructive radiographic lesion requires planned evaluation before biopsy or fixation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Osteosarcoma: adolescence, hereditary retinoblastoma (RB1), prior radiation, Paget disease; chondrosarcoma: older adults
Hereditary multiple exostoses predispose to osteochondromas; most adult malignant bone lesions are metastases

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Night/rest pain**, enlarging mass, constitutional symptoms or pathologic fracture → concerning lesion
Osteoid osteoma: nocturnal pain relieved by NSAIDs; small cortical nidus
Osteochondroma: painless metaphyseal exostosis with medullary continuity; new growth after maturity concerning
Known cancer + constant back pain, vertebral point tenderness → **spinal metastasis**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Tumor lineage determines osteoid, cartilage or primitive-cell production; aggressive growth destroys cortex
Giant cell tumor: neoplastic stromal cells recruit osteoclast-like giant cells, causing locally aggressive osteolysis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Plain radiographs first**; assess location, margins, periosteal reaction and matrix
Aggressive lesion → MRI entire involved bone/adjacent joint; chest CT for lung metastases
★ **Orthopedic oncology plans biopsy tract**; core biopsy after imaging, before definitive treatment
CBC, ESR/CRP if infection suspected; normal labs do not exclude malignancy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Osteosarcoma → **neoadjuvant chemotherapy + wide resection**, then postoperative chemotherapy
Ewing → systemic chemotherapy plus surgery and/or radiation
Chondrosarcoma → wide surgical excision; conventional tumors relatively chemo/radioresistant
Symptomatic osteoid osteoma → radiofrequency ablation; asymptomatic osteochondroma → observation
Giant cell tumor → curettage/reconstruction; selected unresectable lesions → denosumab

rows.label: Complications
items: Pathologic fracture, neurovascular compromise, pulmonary metastases; limb surgery and chemotherapy morbidity
Mandible metastasis → mental nerve anesthesia (**numb chin**)

rows.label: Mimics
items: Osteomyelitis: infection markers, cultures; may closely resemble Ewing
Bone metastases: older adult, multiple lesions; myeloma: anemia, monoclonal protein
Unicameral bone cyst: child, lucent expansile proximal humerus lesion; pathologic fracture after minor trauma

bone-tumors.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

bowel-obstruction.name: Bowel obstruction
bowel-obstruction.scope: Small bowel obstruction (adhesions, hernia), large bowel obstruction (volvulus, malignancy), paralytic ileus, NG decompression, surgical management
bowel-obstruction.core: Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, distention, and obstipation suggest mechanical obstruction; constant pain or systemic toxicity raises concern for strangulation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior abdominal surgery (**adhesions**, leading cause), incarcerated hernia, Crohn strictures → small-bowel obstruction
Colorectal malignancy, chronic constipation, institutionalization → large-bowel obstruction or sigmoid volvulus
Recent surgery, opioids, hypokalemia, severe systemic illness → ileus

rows.label: Clues
items: Early high-pitched sounds may become absent; proximal obstruction causes earlier vomiting, distal disease greater distention
★ **Peritonitis, fever, tachycardia, rising lactate**, or continuous severe pain → ischemia/perforation
Complete → **obstipation**, no flatus; partial may still pass stool/diarrhea, not excluding obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Luminal blockage → upstream dilation, third spacing; closed loop compromises venous then arterial supply
Adynamic ileus reflects impaired motility without an anatomic transition point

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast** defines transition point, cause, and ischemic signs
CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, lactate; normal lactate cannot exclude early ischemia
Radiograph may show dilated loops/air-fluid levels, no rectal gas; CT more definitive if diagnosis uncertain
★ Massive colonic distention + **coffee-bean (inverted-U) loop** on radiograph → sigmoid volvulus
Pregnancy: plain radiograph acceptable first (minimal fetal dose); MRI if unclear; do not delay

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO, IV isotonic fluids, electrolyte correction**; NG decompression for significant vomiting/distention
★ Strangulation, perforation, closed loop, or incarcerated hernia → **urgent surgery** + ceftriaxone/metronidazole
Uncomplicated adhesive SBO → surgical observation, serial examination; water-soluble contrast helps predict resolution
Failure to improve during a short monitored trial, commonly up to 72 h → operation
Ileus → correct trigger, reduce opioids, mobilize; no operation solely for absent sounds

rows.label: Complications
items: Dehydration, AKI, hypokalemic alkalosis; bowel necrosis, perforation, sepsis
Recurrent adhesions; short-bowel syndrome after extensive resection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early postoperative ambulation, opioid-sparing analgesia, electrolyte correction; elective repair of symptomatic hernias

rows.label: Mimics
items: Gastroenteritis: prominent diarrhea, no focal transition point
Mesenteric ischemia: pain out of proportion before peritoneal signs
Ileus: hypoactive/absent sounds, gas throughout bowel including rectum
Diabetic autonomic neuropathy: dysmotility, dilated loops without transition point

table.title: Large-bowel branches
rows: Sigmoidoscopic detorsion, rectal tube → same-admission resection

bowel-obstruction.evidence: Not checked online; established acute surgical management principles.

brain-death.name: Brain death
brain-death.scope: Prerequisites (normothermia, normal BP), clinical exam (coma, absent brainstem reflexes), apnea test, ancillary testing (cerebral blood flow studies)
brain-death.core: Permanent loss of all brain function, including brainstem function, constitutes death; a beating heart on ventilation does not negate the diagnosis.

rows.label: Principle
items: Known catastrophic irreversible brain injury; compatible neuroimaging; adequate observation period
No family consent needed; after declaration → stop ventilator, unless organ donation planned

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Prerequisites: **temperature ≥36°C**, adult SBP ≥100 and MAP ≥75 mm Hg
Exclude paralysis/metabolic confounders; sedatives: ≥5 half-lives, longer if impaired clearance
★ Examination: **coma**, no brain-mediated motor response; absent brainstem reflexes (table)

rows.label: Don't
items: Oculocephalic testing with possible cervical injury; use caloric testing after confirming ear integrity
Declare death with any brain-mediated response or spontaneous breath
Use ancillary testing to bypass hypothermia or high CNS-depressant levels

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Spinal reflex movements may persist without contradicting diagnosis
Incomplete examination or unsafe apnea test → radionuclide cerebral perfusion or catheter angiography
After temperature ≤35.5°C, wait ≥24 hours following rewarming to ≥36°C

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Apnea test: no breaths, **PaCO2 ≥60 and ≥20 above baseline**, pH <7.30
Preoxygenate; abort apnea testing for hypotension, hypoxemia or unstable arrhythmia
★ 2023 update: **EEG no longer accepted** as ancillary testing; pediatric requirements differ

brain-tumors.name: Brain tumors
brain-tumors.scope: Metastatic brain tumors, glioblastoma, meningioma, pediatric tumors (medulloblastoma), vestibular schwannoma
brain-tumors.core: Progressive focal deficits, new seizures or headache with raised intracranial pressure require brain imaging for a mass lesion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Known lung, breast, melanoma, renal or colorectal malignancy → brain metastases
Prior cranial radiation; NF 2 predisposes to bilateral vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning headache, vomiting, papilledema; altered consciousness or pupillary asymmetry → impending herniation
Frontal → personality change; posterior fossa → ataxia; temporal (Meyer loop) → contralateral **superior quadrantanopia**
Pediatric posterior fossa mass can obstruct CSF flow and rapidly cause hydrocephalus
★ **Anosmia**, normal nasal exam, frontal release signs, papilledema → **subfrontal olfactory groove meningioma**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Tumor disrupts local brain function and blood–brain barrier → vasogenic edema
Fixed cranial volume makes expanding tissue/CSF raise pressure and threaten brainstem perfusion
Astrocytoma grade, prognosis → **degree of histologic anaplasia**, not metastasis; extracranial spread rare

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Contrast MRI brain** best defines mass, edema and multiplicity; CT for unstable patients
Metastatic pattern → search primary with chest/abdominal imaging; tissue diagnosis when needed
★ Suspected mass with pressure signs → **avoid LP** until safe after imaging
Tinnitus, imbalance, facial weakness/numbness, altered taste (CN VII, V) → audiometry and MRI internal auditory canals

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic edema → **dexamethasone**; herniation → head elevation, hypertonic saline/mannitol, emergency neurosurgery
Seizure → levetiracetam; no routine antiseizure prophylaxis for every seizure-naive tumor patient
★ **Resection versus radiation** depends on lesion, symptoms, accessibility and systemic disease
Medulloblastoma → resection, chemotherapy and usually craniospinal radiation; avoid/delay radiation in very young children
Craniopharyngioma resection disrupts pituitary stalk → **lifelong pituitary hormone replacement**; watch central DI

rows.label: Complications
items: Obstructive hydrocephalus, herniation, hemorrhage, persistent neurologic deficits
Radiation injury, cognitive decline, steroid hyperglycemia and infection

rows.label: Mimics
items: Abscess: infection context and central diffusion restriction
Primary CNS lymphoma: often periventricular; steroids can obscure biopsy
Stroke: abrupt maximal onset with vascular distribution; chronic subdural: prior head trauma
Ménière disease: episodic vertigo, fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss

table.title: Tumor distinctions
rows: Months of headache, deficits; necrotic, crosses corpus callosum
Woman; extra-axial, uniform enhancement, dural tail; parasagittal
Child; midline cerebellar mass; CSF drop metastases
CPA; insidious, high-frequency unilateral sensorineural hearing loss
Child; ataxia, nystagmus, head tilt, cranial neuropathies

brain-tumors.evidence: Not checked online; established neuro-oncology teaching.

breast-cancer-screening.name: Breast cancer screening
breast-cancer-screening.scope: USPSTF screening mammography recommendations, age-based intervals, high-risk screening (BRCA, prior chest radiation, breast MRI), clinical breast exam, diagnostic evaluation of abnormal screening
breast-cancer-screening.core: USPSTF recommends biennial mammography from ages 40–74 for average-risk women; symptoms require diagnostic evaluation regardless of screening schedule.

rows.label: Who
items: Average risk includes family history or dense breasts without a defined high-risk syndrome
★ BRCA pathogenic variant, young chest irradiation or lifetime risk **≥20–25%** → high-risk pathway

rows.label: Start/stop
items: Age ≥75: insufficient USPSTF evidence; individualize by health, life expectancy and preference
High risk: annual MRI plus mammography, typically around age 30; specialist-tailored earlier MRI
BRCA1/2: **bilateral mastectomy + salpingo-oophorectomy** = greatest risk reduction; tamoxifen weaker

rows.label: Test
items: ★ Digital mammography/tomosynthesis; **MRI supplements**, not replaces, high-risk mammography
Clinical breast examination and breast self-examination do not substitute for imaging

rows.label: IF positive
items: ★ BI-RADS 0 → **diagnostic views/targeted ultrasound**; 4–5 → core needle biopsy
BI-RADS 3 → short-interval imaging, usually 6 months; 1–2 → routine interval
Palpable concerning mass with negative imaging → tissue assessment for clinical–radiologic discordance

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Older teaching: 50; **2024 USPSTF starts at 40**; other societies accept annual
Dense breasts alone: insufficient USPSTF evidence for routine supplemental ultrasound/MRI
Harms: false positives, biopsy, overdiagnosis; concerning mass needs evaluation despite normal mammogram

breast-neoplasia.name: Breast neoplasia
breast-neoplasia.scope: Ductal carcinoma in situ, invasive ductal and lobular carcinoma, receptor status (ER, PR, HER2), metastatic disease (bone, visceral), surgical management, endocrine and chemotherapy
breast-neoplasia.core: A suspicious breast lesion requires core biopsy, assessment of invasion and ER/PR/HER2 status to guide local and systemic treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Increasing age, BRCA-related syndromes, close-relative family history (distant relative adds little), prior chest irradiation
**Combined estrogen-progestin therapy**, prolonged estrogen, postmenopausal obesity, alcohol; atypical proliferative lesions

rows.label: Clues
items: Painless hard irregular mass, skin/nipple retraction, unilateral bloody discharge or axillary node
★ Peau d’orange, diffuse erythema and edema → **inflammatory breast cancer**, even without discrete mass
Persistent unilateral eczematous nipple lesion → Paget disease; **full-thickness biopsy**, investigate underlying carcinoma

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Invasion through basement membrane enables lymphatic/hematogenous metastasis
ER/PR signaling and HER2 amplification create actionable tumor drivers; triple-negative tumors lack these targets

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Diagnostic mammography + targeted ultrasound** → core biopsy of suspicious lesion; pregnancy → **ultrasound first**
Pathology: invasion, grade, **ER/PR/HER2**; assess regional nodes clinically and with targeted imaging
Clinically node-negative invasive disease, including microinvasion ≤1 mm → sentinel node biopsy during definitive surgery
Distant staging scans for advanced disease or suspicious symptoms; not every small asymptomatic cancer
Axillary node adenocarcinoma, normal mammogram → occult breast primary; breast MRI

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Early: lumpectomy + radiation or mastectomy; **positive margins → reexcision** before adjuvant therapy
ER-positive → tamoxifen or postmenopausal aromatase inhibitor; chemotherapy based on stage/biology
★ HER2-positive → **trastuzumab-based** treatment, monitor LVEF; triple-negative → chemotherapy ± pembrolizumab if higher-risk
Locally advanced → neoadjuvant treatment, then surgery/radiation; large residual + palpable nodes → **mastectomy + axillary dissection**
Bone metastases → **zoledronate/denosumab**; systemic treatment by receptors, chemotherapy for visceral crisis

rows.label: Complications
items: Metastases to bone (often **mixed lytic–blastic**), lung, liver, brain; surgery/radiation → lymphedema
Tamoxifen → VTE/endometrial cancer; aromatase inhibitors → bone loss; trastuzumab → cardiomyopathy
Prior cancer + severe hypercalcemia, lytic lesions → recurrence; thiazide/calcium supplements cause only mild elevation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Age/risk-based screening, genetic counseling for suggestive pedigree; selected high-risk patients → chemoprevention
BRCA-related very high risk → discuss risk-reducing surgery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Mastitis: lactation-associated tenderness/fever, improves with antibiotics
Fat necrosis: trauma/surgery history; biopsy if discordant imaging

table.title: Histologic distinctions
rows: Bilateral risk marker; discohesive lobular cells
Surveillance/risk reduction if concordant; later cancer usually ductal

breast-neoplasia.evidence: Not checked online; established breast-oncology management principles.

candidiasis.name: Candidiasis
candidiasis.scope: Oropharyngeal candidiasis (thrush), diaper candidiasis, intertrigo, vulvovaginal candidiasis, cell-mediated vs neutrophil immunity, nystatin, fluconazole
candidiasis.core: Opportunistic yeast overgrowth on mucosa or moist skin; distribution and host immune defects determine evaluation and antifungal route.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Recent antibiotics, diabetes, pregnancy, inhaled/systemic steroids, HIV; infants, dentures, skin occlusion
Neutropenia, central venous catheters, parenteral nutrition → invasive infection risk

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Odynophagia or dysphagia with immunosuppression** → esophageal involvement, even without visible oral lesions
Persistent/recurrent thrush outside infancy → evaluate HIV, diabetes, or other immune defects
Sepsis in neutropenic or catheterized host → consider candidemia rather than isolated superficial disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ★ **T-cell/IL-17 dysfunction → mucocutaneous disease; neutrophil defects → invasive candidiasis**
Candida albicans: budding yeast and pseudohyphae; overgrowth of endogenous flora rather than routine sexual transmission

rows.label: Dx
items: Typical oral/cutaneous disease → clinical diagnosis; uncertain lesions → KOH microscopy
★ Vaginal symptoms → wet mount/KOH; **pH usually <4.5**; negative microscopy with suspicion → culture
Complicated/recurrent vaginitis → culture/speciation; asymptomatic colonization alone needs no treatment

rows.label: Tx
items: Esophageal disease → **systemic fluconazole 14–21 days**; refractory symptoms → endoscopy with biopsy
★ Pregnancy → **7-day intravaginal clotrimazole**; systemic triazoles contraindicated
Recurrent vaginitis ≥3 episodes/year → extended induction then weekly fluconazole for 6 months
Candidemia → IV micafungin and blood cultures; investigate/remove infected catheter

rows.label: Complications
items: Poor oral intake, painful fissures, recurrent vaginitis; invasive disease → endophthalmitis, endocarditis, organ abscesses
Azoles: hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation, CYP interactions

rows.label: Prevention
items: Rinse mouth after inhaled steroids; clean dentures, keep folds dry, change wet diapers promptly
Optimize glucose control and HIV ART; routine partner treatment unnecessary for uncomplicated vaginitis

rows.label: Mimics
items: Leukoplakia/oral hairy leukoplakia: white plaques do not scrape off
Irritant diaper dermatitis: spares folds; bacterial vaginosis: fishy odor, elevated vaginal pH

table.title: Superficial presentations
rows: Beefy erythema, satellite pustules; folds involved
Topical azole or single-dose oral fluconazole

cardiomyopathies.name: Cardiomyopathies
cardiomyopathies.scope: Dilated cardiomyopathy, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, restrictive cardiomyopathy, stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy, viral myocarditis, diagnostic evaluation, management
cardiomyopathies.core: Myocardial disease causes pump failure, impaired filling, dynamic obstruction, or arrhythmias; echocardiography defines the phenotype.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Dilated: familial disease, alcohol, anthracyclines, peripartum state, **viral myocarditis**
Hypertrophic: autosomal dominant sarcomeric variants; restrictive: amyloid, hemochromatosis, radiation
Takotsubo: emotional/physical stress; myocarditis: recent viral illness, immune checkpoint inhibitors

rows.label: Clues
items: Exertional dyspnea, edema, elevated JVP; **displaced PMI**, S3 → dilated LV; syncope/ventricular arrhythmia signals danger
★ Obstructive HCM murmur **↑Valsalva/standing**, ↓squatting/handgrip; exertional presyncope
Myocarditis: chest discomfort, tachycardia disproportionate to fever, acute heart failure

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Sarcomere dysfunction or myocardial injury → remodeling; infiltration → reduced ventricular compliance

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ECG, troponin, BNP → transthoracic echo**; assess coronary ischemia when suspected
Cardiac MRI: inflammation, scar, infiltrative patterns; iron studies or monoclonal protein testing when relevant
Endomyocardial biopsy: selected fulminant unexplained failure, malignant arrhythmias, suspected giant-cell myocarditis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ HFrEF: **ARNI, evidence-based beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor**; loop diuretic for congestion
Obstructive HCM: nonvasodilating beta-blocker (propranolol, metoprolol); alternative verapamil/diltiazem
Refractory obstruction → myosin inhibitor, disopyramide, or septal reduction; avoid dehydration and vasodilators
